claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about future applications, supported by citations to disease modeling studies.

claims.claim: Digital atlases enable automated segmentation of new images.
claims.source: Finally, digital atlases enable automated segmentation of new images, which is essential for whole brain mapping approaches that can lead to unexpected discoveries of regional function (Bahl and Engert, 2020; Kim et al., 2015; Pantoja et al., 2020; Randlett et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on whole brain mapping.

claims.claim: Automated segmentation is essential for whole brain mapping approaches that can lead to unexpected discoveries of regional function.
claims.source: Finally, digital atlases enable automated segmentation of new images, which is essential for whole brain mapping approaches that can lead to unexpected discoveries of regional function (Bahl and Engert, 2020; Kim et al., 2015; Pantoja et al., 2020; Randlett et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating this capability.

claims.claim: Whole brain activity mapping facilitates powerful network approaches to understanding brain function.
claims.source: Whole brain activity mapping also facilitates powerful network approaches to understanding brain (Bassett and Sporns, 2017; Coelho et al., 2018; Vetere et al., 2017; Wheeler et al., 2013), yielding insight into how coordinated brain-wide activity gives rise to behavior.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on brain network analysis.

claims.claim: The mature adult zebrafish brain is opaque and an order of magnitude larger than the larval brain.
claims.source: The generation of a brain atlas for adult zebrafish presents several challenges in comparison to the larval brain because the mature brain is opaque and an order of magnitude larger; this makes traditional whole-mount approaches impossible and confocal or wide-field microscopy infeasible.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of zebrafish developmental biology and physical properties.

claims.claim: The opacity and size of the adult zebrafish brain makes traditional whole-mount approaches impossible and confocal or wide-field microscopy infeasible.
claims.source: The generation of a brain atlas for adult zebrafish presents several challenges in comparison to the larval brain because the mature brain is opaque and an order of magnitude larger; this makes traditional whole-mount approaches impossible and confocal or wide-field microscopy infeasible.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the physical limitations of these techniques given the properties of adult zebrafish brains.

claims.claim: Adult brains were rendered transparent using a tissue clearing approach (iDISCO+).
claims.source: To enable whole-mount imaging, we rendered adult brains transparent using a tissue clearing approach (iDISCO+) that is compatible with different stains such as small molecules, antibodies, and in situ probes (Kramer et al., 2018; Renier et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, supported by citations to the iDISCO+ technique.

claims.claim: iDISCO+ is compatible with different stains such as small molecules, antibodies, and in situ probes.
claims.source: To enable whole-mount imaging, we rendered adult brains transparent using a tissue clearing approach (iDISCO+) that is compatible with different stains such as small molecules, antibodies, and in situ probes (Kramer et al., 2018; Renier et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on iDISCO+.

claims.claim: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy was used for rapid large volume imaging with minimal photobleaching.
claims.source: High-resolution imaging of samples as large as intact adult brains is not amenable to conventional microscopic techniques, so we turned to light-sheet fluorescence microscopy for rapid large volume imaging with minimal photobleaching (Pitrone et al., 2013; Reynaud et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by citations to prior work on light-sheet microscopy.

claims.claim: 3D volumes from multiple animals were registered into the same anatomical space prior to averaging to generate an atlas that minimizes individual variations in neuroanatomy.
claims.source: To generate an atlas that minimizes individual variations in neuroanatomy, we registered 3D volumes from multiple animals into the same anatomical space prior to averaging (Lerch et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by a citation to prior work on image registration.

claims.claim: Images from 10 different antibody stains were registered into the same anatomical space to help guide segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the brain.
claims.source: To help guide segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the brain, images from 10 different antibody stains were also registered into the same anatomical space.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology and data collected in the study.

claims.claim: Manual segmentation was performed, delineating the atlas into over 200 neuroanatomical regions, including nuclei and white matter tracts.
claims.source: Finally, we performed manual segmentation, delineating the atlas into over 200 neuroanatomical regions, including nuclei and white matter tracts.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology and results of the segmentation process.

claims.claim: AZBA is the most comprehensive, detailed, and up-to-date atlas of the adult zebrafish brain.
claims.source: Taken together, AZBA is the most comprehensive, detailed, and up-to-date atlas of the adult zebrafish brain.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the quality and novelty of the work, inferred from the comprehensive methodology and results presented.

claims.claim: All averaged images are freely available at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g and azba.wayne.edu.
claims.source: We have made all averaged images freely available (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g; azba.wayne.edu) to enable their use in exploring the organization of the zebrafish brain and automated segmentation for activity mapping.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claims.claim: AZBA can be continuously updated to reflect the latest findings in zebrafish neuroanatomy because it was generated using readily available techniques.
claims.source: By generating this resource using readily available techniques, AZBA can be continuously updated to reflect the latest findings in zebrafish neuroanatomy.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the updatability of the resource based on the methodology used.

claims.claim: AZBA will become an indispensable resource as adult zebrafish continue to gain traction as a model organism in understanding the intricacies of the vertebrate brain.
claims.source: We anticipate this becoming an indispensable resource as adult zebrafish continue to gain traction as a model organism in understanding the intricacies of the vertebrate brain.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future impact of the resource.

claims.claim: A whole-mount preparation was used to avoid issues with slice-based techniques such as tissue loss, tearing, and distortion.
claims.source: We used a whole-mount preparation to avoid issues with slice-based techniques such as tissue loss, tearing, and distortion.
claims.evidence: This describes the rationale for the methodology used.

claims.claim: iDISCO+ is a rapid organic solvent-based tissue clearing technique that renders brains optically transparent.
claims.source: To circumvent the challenge of tissue opacity, we used a rapid organic solvent-based tissue clearing technique, iDISCO+ (Renier et al., 2016), that renders brains optically transparent.
claims.evidence: This describes the technique used, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Tissue clearing using iDISCO+ resulted in transparent brains.
claims.source: Tissue clearing using iDISCO+ resulted in transparent brains (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Cleared and stained brains were imaged in the horizontal plane with an in-plane resolution of 3.25 μm and an axial step size of 4 μm.
claims.source: Cleared and stained brains were imaged in the horizontal plane with an in-plane resolution of 3.25 μm and an axial step size of 4 μm (Figure 2B) yielding near-isotropic signals at sufficient resolution to clearly distinguish regional boundaries.
claims.evidence: This describes the imaging parameters used in the study.

claims.claim: The imaging yielded near-isotropic signals at sufficient resolution to clearly distinguish regional boundaries.
claims.source: Cleared and stained brains were imaged in the horizontal plane with an in-plane resolution of 3.25 μm and an axial step size of 4 μm (Figure 2B) yielding near-isotropic signals at sufficient resolution to clearly distinguish regional boundaries.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the imaging parameters and quality of the resulting images.

claims.claim: 17 sets of nuclear-stained and associated autofluorescence images from both male and female fish (eight females) were retained for registration.
claims.source: We retained 17 sets of nuclear-stained and associated autofluorescence images from both male and female fish (eight females), each of which were transformed into 3D volumes for registration.
claims.evidence: This describes the sample size and composition used in the study.

claims.claim: The atlas was generated by registering images from individual animals into the same space, thereby creating an anatomical average.
claims.source: The atlas was generated by registering images from individual animals into the same space, thereby creating an anatomical average.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used to create the atlas.

claims.claim: The image registration approach has been previously used in humans, mice, macaques, and zebrafish larvae.
claims.source: This approach has been previously used in humans (Klein et al., 2009), mice (Dorr et al., 2008; Steadman et al., 2014), macaques (McLaren et al., 2009), and zebrafish larvae (Kunst et al., 2019; Randlett et al., 2015; Ronneberger et al., 2012; Tabor et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work using similar registration approaches.

claims.claim: The registration method begins with a 6-parameter linear registration to rotate and translate the initial image dataset.
claims.source: This method begins with a 6-parameter linear registration to rotate and translate the initial image dataset followed by a 12-parameter affine registration to scale, translate, rotate, and shear the dataset with a pairwise approach to avoid bias by outlier images (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: A 12-parameter affine registration was performed to scale, translate, rotate, and shear the dataset with a pairwise approach to avoid bias by outlier images.
claims.source: This method begins with a 6-parameter linear registration to rotate and translate the initial image dataset followed by a 12-parameter affine registration to scale, translate, rotate, and shear the dataset with a pairwise approach to avoid bias by outlier images (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: An iterative nonlinear registration with six iterations at subsequently higher resolutions was performed using minctracc.
claims.source: Lastly, an iterative nonlinear registration with six iterations at subsequently higher resolutions was performed using minctracc (Collins and Evans, 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by a citation to the minctracc tool.

claims.claim: The registration resulted in a set of linear and nonlinear transformations for each TO-PRO image from native space to a consensus space and orientation.
claims.source: This resulted in a set of linear and nonlinear transformations for each TO-PRO image in our dataset from native space to a consensus space and orientation.
claims.evidence: This describes the output of the registration process.

claims.claim: The transformations were applied to corresponding autofluorescence images, creating an atlas with averaged images containing TO-PRO and autofluorescence signals.
claims.source: These transformations were then applied to corresponding autofluorescence images, thereby creating an atlas with averaged images containing TO-PRO and autofluorescence signals (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology and results, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Images were acquired using 10 different antibody stains to provide additional guidance for segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the adult zebrafish brain.
claims.source: To provide additional guidance for segmentation and generate insight into the neurochemical organization of the adult zebrafish brain, we also acquired images using 10 different antibody stains (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology and rationale for using antibody stains.

claims.claim: The antibody stains used identify different cell types in the brain, such as neurons (HuC/D), radial glial cells (GFAP), and proliferating cells (PCNA).
claims.source: We sought stains that would identify different cell types in the brain, such as neurons (HuC/D), radial glial cells (glial fibrillary associated protein [GFAP]), and proliferating cells (proliferating cell nuclear antigen [PCNA]), markers for different neurotransmitters (tyrosine hydroxylase [TH], 5-hydroxytryptamine [5-HT], and choline acetyltransferase [ChAT]), and calcium binding proteins (parvalbumin [PV], calbindin, and calretinin).
claims.evidence: This describes the types of antibody stains used and their targets.

claims.claim: Some antibody stains, such as TH, 5-HT, ChAT, and calretinin, have already been subject to brain-wide analysis, making them useful for guiding segmentation.
claims.source: Some of these stains, such as TH, 5-HT, ChAT, and calretinin, have already been subject to brain-wide analysis, making them useful for guiding segmentation.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge from prior literature on these stains.

claims.claim: Autofluorescence images from antibody stains were registered with the autofluorescence channel of the TO-PRO images to bring antibody stains into the same anatomical space as the TO-PRO stain.
claims.source: Autofluorescence images from antibody stains were registered with the autofluorescence channel of the TO-PRO images, yielding a set of transformations that were used to bring antibody stains into the same anatomical space as the TO-PRO stain (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: At least five independent brains were averaged together to generate a representative image for each antibody.
claims.source: To generate a representative image for each antibody, we averaged together at least five independent brains.
claims.evidence: This describes the sample size used for each antibody stain.

claims.claim: The approach resulted in strong correspondence between antibody images and the TO-PRO stain.
claims.source: Our approach resulted in strong correspondence between antibody images and the TO-PRO stain (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the registration quality, illustrated in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Using a mixed-model ANOVA, a main effect of signal was found (F(1,13) = 1084, p=6.6 × 10–14) with the TO-PRO signal having greater mean precision (15 ± 10 µm vs. 99 ± 53 µm).
claims.source: Using a mixed-model ANOVA (2 × 15; signal [between subject] × landmark [within subject]), we found a main effect of signal (F(1,13) = 1084, p=6.6 × 10–14) with the TO-PRO signal having greater mean precision (15 ± 10 µm vs. 99 ± 53 µm; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of registration precision data.

claims.claim: There was a significant effect of landmark (F(5,65) = 98, p<2 × 10–16) and an interaction between signal and landmark (F(5, 65) = 120, p<2 × 10–16) in registration precision.
claims.source: However, there was also a significant effect of landmark (F(5,65) = 98, p<2 × 10–16), and an interaction between signal and landmark (F(5, 65) = 120, p<2 × 10–16).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of registration precision data.

claims.claim: In the autofluorescence images, the average precision of each landmark covers a much wider range (17–180 µm) than TO-PRO (9–23 µm).
claims.source: A closer examination of the data revealed that in the autofluorescence images the average precision of each landmark covers a much wider range (17–180 µm) than TO-PRO (9–23 µm).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the registration precision data.

claims.claim: The larger error measured using autofluorescence images is likely due to experimenter error in selecting points, reflecting the paucity of well-defined landmarks in this signal compared to the richer, high-contrast TO-PRO images.
claims.source: This suggests that the larger error measured using autofluorescence images is likely due to experimenter error in selecting points, reflecting the paucity of well-defined landmarks in this signal compared to the richer, high-contrast TO-PRO images.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of the precision data.

claims.claim: Segmentation was primarily guided by the seminal atlas of Wullimann et al., 1996.
claims.source: Segmentation was primarily guided by the seminal atlas of Wullimann et al., 1996.
claims.evidence: This describes the primary reference used for segmentation.

claims.claim: Regional boundaries and terminology were updated for parts of the brain that have been subject to more recent analysis such as the telencephalon, hypothalamic regions, and motor nuclei.
claims.source: Regional boundaries and terminology were updated for parts of the brain that have been subject to more recent analysis such as the telencephalon, hypothalamic regions, and motor nuclei (Mueller et al., 2004; Porter and Mueller, 2020; Rink and Wullimann, 2001).
claims.evidence: This describes updates to the segmentation based on more recent literature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Segmenting large, clearly delineated regions, such as the optic tectum and the cerebellum, was straightforward.
claims.source: Segmenting large, clearly delineated regions, such as the optic tectum and the cerebellum, was straightforward (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the segmentation process.

claims.claim: Small nuclei that only appear in one or two slices in the atlas or in images from only one axis proved more challenging to segment.
claims.source: Small nuclei that only appear in one or two slices in the atlas or in images from only one axis proved more challenging.
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the challenges in the segmentation process.

claims.claim: The coronal axis was primarily used for segmenting small nuclei due to it being the most extensively represented in both the atlas and the literature.
claims.source: For such regions, we primarily made use of the coronal axis due to it being the most extensively represented in both the atlas and the literature (Figure 5A, bottom).
claims.evidence: This describes the rationale for using the coronal axis in segmentation.

claims.claim: A neuronal marker (HuC/D) was used in conjunction with the nuclear stain to safely identify many boundaries.
claims.source: To ensure we captured as many neuronal structures as possible, we also made extensive use of a neuronal marker (HuC/D) in conjunction with the nuclear stain, which allowed us to safely identify many boundaries (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology used for segmentation.

claims.claim: The original brain atlas contains a significant amount of unsegmented space.
claims.source: Other challenges included the fact that the original brain atlas contains a significant amount of unsegmented space.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of the prior atlas.

claims.claim: Unsegmented regions were labeled as 'unknown' and according to their lowest anatomical level.
claims.source: We labeled these regions as 'unknown' and according to their lowest anatomical level (e.g., unknown ventral telencephalon [UnkVT], unknown diencephalon [UnkD], etc.).
claims.evidence: This describes the labeling convention used for unsegmented regions.

claims.claim: Identification of tracts was largely based on a combination of autofluorescence and lack of nuclear and neuronal staining since a white matter stain compatible with iDISCO+ was not found.
claims.source: Identification of tracts was largely based on a combination of autofluorescence and lack of nuclear and neuronal staining since we were unsuccessful in finding a white matter stain compatible with iDISCO+ (e.g., the MLF: Figure 4D, pink arrowheads).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology and challenges in identifying white matter tracts.

claims.claim: All immunostainings showed high overlap with prior work, establishing the validity of these antibodies.
claims.source: All of our immunostainings showed high overlap with prior work, establishing the validity of these antibodies (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative assessment of the antibody staining results compared to prior literature.

claims.claim: Extensive TH expression was found in the olfactory bulb and as a continuous band ventral to the Dc region in the telencephalon.
claims.source: For example, in the telencephalon we found extensive TH expression in the olfactory bulb (Figure 5Ba), and as a continuous band ventral to the Dc region (Figure 5Bb).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed TH expression pattern, shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: TH staining was elevated in the optic tectum, thalamic, and hypothalamic regions, the LC, and in the XLo of the hindbrain.
claims.source: As previously reported, TH staining was also elevated in the optic tectum, thalamic, and hypothalamic regions (Figure 5Bc,d), the LC (Figure 5Be), and in the XLo of the hindbrain (Figure 5Bf).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed TH expression pattern, consistent with prior reports.

claims.claim: 5-HT staining was more diffuse in regions like the optic tectum and the dorsal part of the telencephalon, with pockets of high expression restricted to regions like the PVO, PTN, posterior portion of the Hc, and the SR.
claims.source: We found 5-HT staining to be more diffuse in regions like the optic tectum and the dorsal part of the telencephalon (Figure 5Ca,b), with pockets of high expression restricted to regions like the PVO (Figure 5Cc), PTN (Figure 5Cd), posterior portion of the Hc (Figure 5Ce), and the SR (Figure 5Cf).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed 5-HT expression pattern, shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: ChAT staining was clearly discerned in places such as the RT, near the TTB, and in the SRN and NLV.
claims.source: Using ChAT, we could clearly discern staining in places such as the RT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Ba), near the TTB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Bb), and in the SRN and NLV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Bc).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed ChAT expression pattern, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: ChAT staining was apparent in several motor nuclei such as the OENr and VIIm, OENc, and IXm.
claims.source: ChAT staining was also apparent in several motor nuclei such as the OENr and VIIm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Bd), OENc (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Be), and IXm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Be).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed ChAT expression pattern in motor nuclei, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: High levels of calretinin staining were seen in the olfactory bulb, the Dm, the PSP and optic tract, optic tectum, the TLa, SG, TGN, and anterior portion of the DIL, with particularly strong staining in the SGN and DON.
claims.source: Finally, examples of high levels of calretinin staining can be seen in the olfactory bulb (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Ca), the Dm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cb), the PSP and optic tract (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cc), optic tectum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cc–e), the TLa, SG, TGN, and anterior portion of the DIL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cd) with particularly strong staining in the SGN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Ce) and DON (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Cf).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed calretinin expression pattern, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The segmentation resulted in a 3D model of the zebrafish brain that can be viewed from any arbitrary angle.
claims.source: Our segmentation resulted in a 3D model of the zebrafish brain that can be viewed from any arbitrary angle (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This describes the output of the segmentation process, illustrated in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Each nucleus, white matter tract, ventricle, and anatomical space was given a unique abbreviation and color, totaling 203 regions.
claims.source: Each nucleus, white matter tract, ventricle, and anatomical space was given a unique abbreviation and color, totaling 203 regions (Supplementary file 1) and associated with an anatomical hierarchy (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This describes the organization and labeling of the segmented regions.

claims.claim: The full extent of the atlas can be appreciated using the website (azba.wayne.edu) or ITK-SNAP.
claims.source: The full extent of the atlas can be appreciated using the website (azba.wayne.edu) or ITK-SNAP (Yushkevich et al., 2019), a freely available software package designed for viewing 3D medical images that allows for the simultaneous viewing of the stains and segmentation in the coronal, sagittal, and horizontal planes (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This describes the tools available for viewing the atlas.

claims.claim: All files for exploring AZBA are freely available for use in ITK-SNAP or other programs at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g.
claims.source: All files for exploring AZBA are freely available for use in ITK-SNAP or other programs (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.dfn2z351g).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claims.claim: Images from both male and female fish were combined to generate a representative brain.
claims.source: Because the goal of the atlas was to generate a representative brain, we combined images from both male and female fish.
claims.evidence: This describes the rationale for combining data from both sexes.

claims.claim: Using a mixed-model ANOVA, neither an effect of sex (F(1,15) = 0.11, p=0.75) nor an interaction between sex and brain region (F(202, 3030) = 0.14, p=1) was found.
claims.source: To determine if there was an effect of sex on brain volumes in our TO-PRO image set, we used a mixed-model ANOVA (2 × 203; sex [between subjects] × brain region [within subjects]). We found neither an effect of sex (F(1,15) = 0.11, p=0.75; Figure 5—figure supplement 2) nor an interaction between sex and brain region (F(202, 3030) = 0.14, p=1; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that sex did not affect the overall size of the brain or individual regions.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of sex differences in brain volumes.

claims.claim: Sex did not affect the overall size of the brain or individual regions.
claims.source: We found neither an effect of sex (F(1,15) = 0.11, p=0.75; Figure 5—figure supplement 2) nor an interaction between sex and brain region (F(202, 3030) = 0.14, p=1; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that sex did not affect the overall size of the brain or individual regions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of brain volumes.

claims.claim: A main effect of region was found (F(202, 3030) = 495, p<2 × 10–16), consistent with the wide range of region sizes observed across the brain (0.000026–0.53 mm3).
claims.source: We did find a main effect of region (F(202, 3030) = 495, p<2 × 10–16), consistent with the wide range of region sizes observed across the brain (0.000026–0.53 mm3; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of regional brain volumes.

claims.claim: Parvalbumin (PV) is a calcium binding protein that labels a class of inhibitory interneurons.
claims.source: Parvalbumin (PV) is a calcium binding protein that labels a class of inhibitory interneurons (Celio, 1986).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on parvalbumin.

claims.claim: Several highly concentrated areas of PV staining were found such as in the anterior portions of the olfactory bulb, APN and DAO, the TSc, the DON and VIII of the hindbrain, and very high levels in the ventral portion of the molecular layer of the cerebellum.
claims.source: We found several highly concentrated areas of PV staining such as in the anterior portions of the olfactory bulb (Figure 7A), APN and DAO (Figure 7Ab), the TSc (Figure 7Ac), the DON and VIII of the hindbrain (Figure 7Af), and very high levels in the ventral portion of the molecular layer of the cerebellum (Figure 7Ad,e) the latter of which likely corresponding with Purkinje and crest cells (Bae et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed PV expression pattern, shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The high PV staining in the ventral portion of the molecular layer of the cerebellum likely corresponds with Purkinje and crest cells.
claims.source: We found several highly concentrated areas of PV staining such as in the anterior portions of the olfactory bulb (Figure 7A), APN and DAO (Figure 7Ab), the TSc (Figure 7Ac), the DON and VIII of the hindbrain (Figure 7Af), and very high levels in the ventral portion of the molecular layer of the cerebellum (Figure 7Ad,e) the latter of which likely corresponding with Purkinje and crest cells (Bae et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed staining pattern and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Prox1 is a homeobox gene critical for regulating neuronal development with widespread expression in larval fish.
claims.source: Prox1 is a homeobox gene critical for regulating neuronal development with widespread expression in larval fish.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Prox1 function.

claims.claim: In juveniles and adult zebrafish, Prox1 expression decreases rapidly and is eventually confined to a relatively few regions.
claims.source: In juveniles and adult zebrafish, Prox1 expression decreases rapidly and is eventually confined to a relatively few regions (Ganz et al., 2012; Pistocchi et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on Prox1 expression.

claims.claim: In the adult zebrafish pallium, Prox1 was reported to be present in the neuronal layer of the Dl with more diffuse staining in posterior portion of the Dc.
claims.source: In the adult zebrafish pallium, Prox1 was reported to be present in the neuronal layer of the Dl with more diffuse staining in posterior portion of the Dc, which we also observed (Figure 7Bb).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed Prox1 expression pattern, consistent with prior reports.

claims.claim: High levels of Prox1 were observed in the olfactory bulb, the habenula, the Val and hypothalamus, and the DIL and the molecular layer of the cerebellum.
claims.source: We also observe high levels of Prox1 in the olfactory bulb (Figure 7Ba), the habenula (Figure 7Bb), the Val and hypothalamus (Figure 7Bd), and the DIL and the molecular layer of the cerebellum (Figure 7Be,f).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed Prox1 expression pattern, shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: PCNA is a marker for proliferating cells.
claims.source: PCNA is a marker for proliferating cells (Grandel et al., 2006; Wullimann and Puelles, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on PCNA.

claims.claim: Consistent with widespread neurogenesis in the adult zebrafish brain, PCNA was found expressed in many neurogenic niches with the highest expression along the midline.
claims.source: Consistent with widespread neurogenesis in the adult zebrafish brain, we found PCNA expressed in many neurogenic niches with the highest expression along the midline (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed PCNA expression pattern, shown in Figure 7C, and relates it to known neurogenesis.

claims.claim: In the telencephalon, a band of high PCNA expression was noticed along the midline in the ventral telencephalon that begins near the olfactory bulbs with a second area in the posterior portion corresponding to the PPa.
claims.source: For example, in the telencephalon we noticed a band of high expression along the midline in the ventral telencephalon that begins near the olfactory bulbs (Figure 7Ca) with a second area in the posterior portion corresponding to the PPa (Figure 7Cb).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed PCNA expression pattern in the telencephalon, shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: High levels of PCNA expression were seen in parts of the thalamus (VM), the hypothalamus (Hd and posterior portion of Hc) and the valvula, caudal lobe, and molecular layers of the cerebellum.
claims.source: We also saw high levels of expression in parts of the thalamus (VM; Figure 7Cc), the hypothalamus (Hd and posterior portion of Hc) and the valvula, caudal lobe, and molecular layers of the cerebellum (Figure 7Cd–f).
claims.evidence: This describes the observed PCNA expression pattern, shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Calbindin is a calcium binding protein important for regulating intracellular signaling that is often used in comparative neurological studies.
claims.source: Calbindin is a calcium binding protein important for regulating intracellular signaling that is often used in comparative neurological studies (Schmidt, 2012).

results.result: The authors created AZBA, the first fully segmented 3D digital atlas of the adult zebrafish brain, by combining tissue clearing (iDISCO+), light-sheet fluorescence microscopy, and 3D image registration. The atlas comprises over 200 neuroanatomical regions segmented from averaged images of 17 brains, with 10 antibody stains registered into the same anatomical space. All data are freely available online and via downloadable files.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C77 collectively describe the creation, methodology, and availability of AZBA. The tissue clearing (C25, C36, C37), light-sheet imaging (C27, C38, C39), registration (C28, C40-C47), antibody staining (C48-C53), and segmentation (C58-C63, C74-C77) are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes, methodological details, and validation against prior atlases. The resource is made publicly available (C32, C77, C139), supporting the claim of creating a comprehensive digital atlas.

results.result: Registration precision was significantly higher using TO-PRO nuclear staining (15 ± 10 µm) compared to autofluorescence (99 ± 53 µm), with significant effects of landmark and signal-landmark interaction. The larger error in autofluorescence is attributed to experimenter error due to fewer well-defined landmarks.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 present statistical analysis of registration precision with appropriate mixed-model ANOVA (F-statistics and p-values provided). The interpretation that autofluorescence error reflects experimenter difficulty in landmark selection (C57) is reasonable given the data showing wider precision ranges (C56). The analysis appropriately uses 6 landmarks across multiple samples.

results.result: Sex did not significantly affect overall brain volume or individual regional volumes in the atlas, with no main effect of sex (F(1,15) = 0.11, p=0.75) or sex-by-region interaction (F(202, 3030) = 0.14, p=1). A significant main effect of region was found, consistent with the wide range of regional volumes (0.000026–0.53 mm³).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 present appropriate statistical analysis using mixed-model ANOVA with adequate sample size (n=17, 8 females). The lack of sex effects (C79, C80) is well-supported by non-significant F-statistics and p-values. The significant regional effect (C81) is expected given anatomical heterogeneity. The decision to combine sexes for the atlas (C78) is justified by these results.

results.result: Antibody staining patterns for neurotransmitter markers (TH, 5-HT, ChAT) and calcium-binding proteins (calretinin, calbindin, PV) showed high correspondence with prior literature, validating the approach. Minor discrepancies in some stains (calbindin, PV) may reflect methodological differences, tissue distortion, or averaging effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C120 demonstrate validation of antibody staining by comparison to extensive prior literature. The observed patterns for TH (C68-C69), 5-HT (C70), ChAT (C71-C72), and calretinin (C73, C116) match previous reports. Minor discrepancies (C117-C118) are acknowledged and plausibly explained (C119). The qualitative validation approach is appropriate for establishing atlas accuracy, though quantitative comparisons would strengthen the claims.

results.result: Novel brain-wide characterization of PV, Prox1, PCNA, calbindin, and GFAP expression patterns revealed specific regional distributions. PV was concentrated in olfactory bulb, cerebellum (likely Purkinje cells), and hindbrain nuclei. PCNA showed widespread expression in neurogenic niches along the midline. GFAP was concentrated near midline/ventricles with some non-ventricular pockets.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C99 describe novel expression patterns for antibodies not previously subject to brain-wide analysis in adult zebrafish. The observations are supported by figures (Figure 7) and are internally consistent. The inference that cerebellar PV corresponds to Purkinje cells (C84) is supported by citation. The PCNA pattern (C90-C92) aligns with known neurogenesis. These represent new descriptive findings enabled by the atlas.

results.result: Prox1 expression in adult zebrafish was found in telencephalon, habenula, hypothalamus, and cerebellum. The lack of overlap between Prox1 and TH in hypothalamus suggests Prox1 is important for development but not maintenance of catecholaminergic neurons. Broader Prox1 expression compared to mice may reflect more widespread adult neurogenesis in zebrafish.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C127 present novel Prox1 expression data with appropriate comparison to prior work (C121-C122, C124, C126). The inference about developmental vs. maintenance roles (C123) is reasonable based on the observed lack of TH/Prox1 overlap. The speculation about neurogenesis (C127) is appropriately tentative and supported by citation. The overlap analysis with GFAP and PCNA (C125) provides additional functional context.

results.result: AZBA represents a significant advance over prior adult zebrafish atlases: the Wullimann et al. (1996) print atlas lacks 3D visualization and updates, while the Ullmann et al. (2010) MRI atlas has limited neurochemical detection and accessibility. AZBA combines widely available techniques for greater versatility and detail.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C104-C111 appropriately contextualize AZBA relative to prior work. The limitations of print atlases (C106) and MRI approaches (C109-C110) are accurately stated. The claim of novelty (C12) is supported by the lack of prior fully segmented 3D digital atlases with comparable detail. The comparison is fair and acknowledges the contributions of prior work (C105) while highlighting AZBA's advantages (C111).

results.result: The authors anticipate AZBA will enhance adult zebrafish research in neuroscience, disease modeling, and functional brain mapping. The atlas is designed to be continuously updated through community contributions, with plans to incorporate additional antibody stains, in situ probes, and transgenic line characterizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C19, C34, C100, C128-C132, C135-C136, C141 are speculative about future impact and applications. While the infrastructure for updates exists (C129), the actual utility and adoption of AZBA for automated segmentation (C136), disease modeling (C19), and community contributions (C131-C132) remain to be demonstrated. These are reasonable expectations but not yet validated results.

results.result: Detailed methods are provided for all aspects of atlas creation, including animal husbandry, tissue preparation, imaging, registration, segmentation, and statistical analysis. Subjects were 15-16 week old AB zebrafish of both sexes, with appropriate ethical approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C159 comprehensively document the methodology with appropriate detail for reproducibility. Sample characteristics (C142-C143), ethical approval (C144), tissue processing (C145-C149), imaging parameters (C150-C152), computational methods (C153-C157), and statistical approaches (C159) are clearly specified with citations to established protocols. Quality control measures (C148) are included.

results.result: The introduction establishes the rationale for AZBA by describing zebrafish as an important neuroscience model organism with advantages over larvae (mature neuroanatomy, complex behaviors), the utility of digital atlases over print versions, and the technical challenges of imaging adult brains (opacity, size).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C24 provide appropriate background and rationale, supported by citations to prior work. The advantages of zebrafish (C1-C3, C13-C14), digital atlases (C15-C22), and challenges of adult brain imaging (C23-C24) are accurately stated based on established knowledge and cited literature. This contextualizes the need for AZBA.

results.result: The original Wullimann atlas contains significant unsegmented space, which was labeled as 'unknown' according to anatomical level in AZBA. White matter tract identification was challenging due to lack of compatible stains, relying on autofluorescence and absence of nuclear/neuronal staining.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 acknowledge limitations in the segmentation process. The labeling of unsegmented regions as 'unknown' (C65) is a transparent approach to handling incomplete prior knowledge. The challenge with white matter identification (C66) is honestly reported, with the methodology used (autofluorescence, negative staining) clearly described. These represent appropriate handling of technical limitations.

results.result: Background information on antibody markers is provided, including their known functions and prior use in zebrafish: TH, 5-HT, ChAT, and calretinin have been subject to brain-wide analysis; PV labels inhibitory interneurons; Prox1 regulates neuronal development; PCNA marks proliferating cells; calbindin regulates intracellular signaling; GFAP marks non-neuronal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C82, C85-C86, C89, C93, C96 provide appropriate background on antibody markers, supported by citations to prior work. This information contextualizes the choice of markers and interpretation of staining patterns. The claims accurately represent established knowledge about these markers.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes AZBA within the broader landscape of model organism atlases, noting similar approaches in larval zebrafish and other species (mice, macaques), while emphasizing the importance of adult-specific data due to developmental changes in expression patterns and the advantages of adult zebrafish (mature neuroanatomy, complex behaviors).
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134, C137, C140 appropriately position AZBA within the field, supported by citations. The comparison to other model organism atlases (C140) and the rationale for adult-specific imaging (C134, C137) are well-justified. These claims provide important context for the significance of the work.
